# SLA Target

`customer_support.obj.core.sla_target` · v1.0.0 · **draft** · scope **core**

> A single running clock attached to a single ticket: a start, a set of conditions under which it pauses, a deadline, and a state. It is not the contract — Entitlement is the contract, and it says only that such a clock exists and how long it is. It is not the ticket either; one ticket carries several SLA Targets at once, and they behave differently enough that sharing a state between them is the defining modelling error of this object. A first-response clock is short, unforgiving, and stops the instant a human replies with anything at all. A resolution clock is long, pauses constantly, and cannot be satisfied by a reply. Fusing them produces a queue that reports health it does not have: every first response met, every resolution late, and one green number covering both.


Also called: `SLA Clock`, `Response Target`, `Resolution Target`, `Service Level Objective`, `SLO`

## Constraints

- **`sla.cannot_exceed_entitlement`** A contractual target cannot be looser than the entitlement it derives from. Tighter is allowed and is an internal choice; looser is a breach of contract dressed as configuration.
- **`sla.pause_only_inside_declared_reasons`** A clock may only pause for a reason the contract names. Pausing for an undeclared reason is unenforceable and will not survive a customer's own timeline of the ticket.
- **`sla.merge_does_not_merge_clocks`** Merging two tickets merges the work and never the clocks. Each original target keeps running against its own start, or the second customer's promise silently disappears into the first customer's ticket.
- **`sla.reopen_starts_a_new_target`** A reopened ticket starts a new target and does not resume the old one. Resuming lets a resolved-then-reopened ticket show a clock that never breached across three weeks of customer pain.
- **`sla.no_clock_outside_coverage`** Counted time cannot accrue outside the coverage window on a business_hours or coverage_window clock — and equally, it cannot be excluded outside a 24/7 one.
- **`sla.breach_is_terminal`** A breached target cannot return to met. Later completion changes the recovery and never the record.


## Business rules

- **`sla.clocks_never_share_a_state`** A first_response target and a resolution target on the same ticket must hold independent clock_state values. Deriving one from the other is prohibited — replying stops the first clock and does nothing at all to the second.

- **`sla.pause_requires_a_reason`** A clock may not enter on_hold with pause_reason = none. An unexplained pause is indistinguishable from a stopped clock and cannot be audited afterwards.
- **`sla.pause_cannot_be_backdated`** pause_started_at may not be set earlier than the moment the pause was recorded. Retroactive pausing is the audit-grade version of the gaming this object is built to see, and it converts a breach into a met target with no trace.

- **`sla.fast_pause_is_reviewable`** A pause beginning within an hour of the customer's last message, on a clock that was already running, is flagged for review. Legitimate, common, and the exact shape of question-laddering — which is why this is a warning and not a block.

- **`sla.breach_must_be_acknowledged`** A breached target must set breach_acknowledged before the ticket can close. The acknowledgement, not the recovery, is what the customer scores — and an unacknowledged breach teaches the organisation nothing.

- **`sla.met_with_negative_sentiment_is_not_a_success`** A target that stops inside its deadline while sentiment is negative must be recorded as met_but_unsatisfied, never as a plain success. This is a measurement failure and belongs in the SLA review, not in the CSAT review.

- **`sla.target_must_derive_from_entitlement`** A target with is_contractual = true and a null entitlement_ref is invalid. We cannot owe a contractual response under a contract we cannot name.
- **`sla.credit_exposure_null_is_not_zero`** A null credit_exposure means the commercial consequence is unknown and must never be reported as no exposure. Same trap as an unverified approval limit, same cost.

## Actions

- **Send a substantive reply** (human) — Stops a first-response clock. Note it stops it whether or not the reply helps, which is the flaw in first-response as a metric and the reason update_cadence exists as a separate target_type.
- **Resume a paused clock** (system) — Restarts counted time when the customer comes back. Should be automatic — a manual resume is a resume that does not happen on a Friday evening.
- **Challenge a recorded pause** (human) — Reinstate the disputed minutes. Belongs to QA or an account review, never to the agent who recorded the pause.
- **Escalate while it is still rescuable** (human) — The only escalation trigger nobody argues with. Almost always fired too late to be an escalation and just early enough to be a warning.
- **Tell the customer before they notice** (human) — The highest-return action on this object. Being told we are late is a service failure; discovering it is a trust failure, and the two recover at completely different speeds.
- **Replace the promise with one we can keep** (human) — Sets a new commitment. Legitimate once, corrosive twice — a second reset teaches the customer that our dates are decorative.
- **Ask the customer to agree to a hold** (human) — Converts a unilateral pause into a mutual one. Slower, and it is the difference between a pause that survives a QBR and one that does not.
- **Move the target** (human) — The correct response to a persistent met_but_unsatisfied pattern. Also the most abused action here — moving a target to stop breaching is only honest when the number was measuring the wrong thing, not when the number was inconvenient.


## Evidence

- **contract** · 10000 bp — What was actually promised, including which minutes count. Nothing outranks it, and it is consulted far less often than it is cited.
- **ticket** · 9000 bp — The platform's own clock record. Authoritative on what the system did — silent on whether the pauses in it were earned.
- **telemetry** · 8500 bp — Timestamps from the systems themselves. Immune to the recording behaviour this object is suspicious of, which is exactly what makes it valuable here.
- **email** · 7500 bp — Thread shape — who wrote when, who was waiting. The whole executable basis of this object today, and inferential by nature.
- **survey** · 7000 bp — Whether meeting the number meant anything. Weak on the mechanics, decisive on whether the mechanics were worth measuring.
- **status_page** · 6000 bp — Declared maintenance and incident windows. Corroborates an exclusion; cannot establish one that the contract does not allow.
- **derived** · 4500 bp — Inferred clock state from thread and sentiment. Corroborating only. Everything executable in this file sits here, and the confidences say so.
- **manual_entry** · 3000 bp — An agent-typed pause reason. Weakest, most consequential, and the only evidence source on this object with an incentive attached — which is precisely why it is scored below inference.


## Metrics

- **attainment_rate** (percent) — Share of targets met. The headline number, and on its own the most misleading metric in support.
- **paused_share_of_elapsed** (percent) — Paused minutes as a share of wall-clock time. The honest companion to attainment — the two move in opposite directions when a queue starts gaming.
- **disputable_pause_rate** (percent) — Share of pauses beginning within an hour of a customer message. Team level only; per-agent it teaches people to stop asking necessary questions.
- **unnoticed_breach_rate** (percent) — Breaches with no follow-up within two days. The number to fix first — it is small, cheap and it is the one customers leave over.
- **proactive_notification_lead** (hours) — Hours between us knowing we will be late and telling them. Negative means they found out first.
- **met_but_unsatisfied_share** (percent) — Targets met over unhappy customers. A measurement-quality metric, not a performance one — it grades the targets, not the team.
- **time_to_first_reply** (hours) — Wall-clock hours from customer message to our reply, pauses ignored. The customer's own version of the number.
- **breach_depth_median** (minutes) — Median minutes past target. Distinguishes a queue that is slightly late from one that is losing tickets.


## Examples

- **Enterprise sev-1, one-hour first response, 24/7** — calendar_hours, is_contractual true, real credit exposure. The clock everybody watches and the one least likely to breach, because it is the only one anybody staffs for.
- **Standard-tier, four business hours, ticket raised 16:55 Friday** — Not due until Monday morning under the contract, and the customer will experience four hours of promise as sixty-three hours of silence. Contractually met, reputationally a breach — the strongest argument in the file for outcome_quality existing.
- **The clarifying question at 15:49 on a four-hour clock started at 12:00** — pause_is_disputable true. Buys a full business day at zero cost, may be entirely legitimate, and is indistinguishable from the alternative in any single ticket. Only the pattern across a queue means anything.
- **Resolution clock on a ticket parked in waiting_on_customer for three weeks** — Ticket state and clock state agree; both are wrong. Nobody chased, the pause was never reviewed, and the ticket auto-closed green. The commonest way a support queue reports health it does not have.
- **Missed callback: 'I'll come back to you Thursday', no contact by Saturday** — No SLA breached at all — the contractual clock may still be running. The commitment breached, and the customer cannot tell the difference and would not care if they could.
- **Incident-linked ticket where service was restored before the fix shipped** — restoration met, resolution still running. Reporting one number for both makes the team look either much better or much worse than it was, depending on which one you picked.
- **Every clock met, CSAT 2/5** — met_but_unsatisfied. The targets are measuring the wrong thing for this ticket type. The right response is recalibrate_target; the common response is coaching the agent, and it fixes nothing.

## Metadata

owner **Customer Support** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional** · completeness **partial**


> Seven of fifteen patterns are executable, which is high for this domain and needs the justification given in the header: elapsed-time predicates (hours_since / days_since) plus thread.ball_in_court are the one clock-shaped primitive the substrate has, and this object is a clock. Every executable pattern here is a proxy and each note names the direction in which its proxy is weak — mostly in the direction that flatters us, which is the bias worth stating.
The two highest-value asks this object generates are sla.target_first_response_at (the real deadline, which every executable pattern above is impersonating) and csat.score (the only thing that can falsify an SLA programme at all — without it "we hit our targets" is unfalsifiable, which is exactly why targets get set where they can be hit).
State names are drawn from vocabulary open.object_states to avoid warnings: `on_hold` is the paused clock and `closed` means met. That mapping loses a little precision against running/paused/met and is documented at the top of the states section rather than fixed by editing the shared vocabulary from inside a single object file.
Two thresholds are guesses and should be recalibrated before anyone trusts them: the -0.2 on derived.sentiment (an engine-computed balance never tuned for support conversations) and the 48 hours in sla.two_days_of_our_silence (set wide on purpose so it fires only on cases that breach under any plausible entitlement).
